etymology: The doctrinal confession of the Church of England, finalized in 1571; thirty-nine articles of religion.
biblical_def: The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion are the doctrinal confession of the Church of England, finalized in 1571, which set the reformed and Protestant character of the English church over against Rome on the one hand and against the radical sects on the other. In their best and clearest articles they confess truly Reformation doctrine: the sufficiency of Holy Scripture for salvation, so that nothing is to be required as an article of faith that is not read therein nor may be proved thereby; justification by faith only, declared a most wholesome doctrine and very full of comfort; the bondage of the will and the necessity of grace; predestination and election as the everlasting purpose of God; and the rejection of Roman errors—the sacrifice of the mass, purgatory, transubstantiation, the invocation of saints, and the like—as repugnant to the Word of God. On these heads the Articles stand within the Reformed confessional family, kin to the continental confessions. Yet the English settlement retained an episcopal government and a prescribed liturgy that the Puritans and nonconformists judged to fall short of a thorough reformation according to the Word; and the comprehensiveness designed to hold together varied parties has allowed later readings that strain against the Articles’ plain Protestant sense. The dictionary honors the Thirty-Nine Articles for their clear confession of Scripture’s sufficiency, justification by faith alone, sovereign grace, and the rejection of Roman corruptions, while noting that the English settlement’s retained ceremonies and prelacy were the very points the nonconformists could not in conscience accept.
webster_summary: The doctrinal confession of the Church of England (1571); clear on Scripture’s sufficiency, justification by faith, and sovereign grace, yet retaining ceremonies the Puritans refused.

corruption_summary: The Articles are read either as crypto-Catholic or as a dead formality; their plain sense is Reformation doctrine, though the English settlement kept ceremonies the Puritans refused.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the later reading, pressed by the Anglo-Catholic movement, that strains the Articles toward Rome—reinterpreting their plain Protestant statements on justification, the mass, and the sacraments in a Catholic sense their framers expressly excluded. The Articles themselves resist this: they call the Romish doctrine of purgatory, pardons, and the adoration of images a fond thing vainly invented, and the sacrifices of masses blasphemous fables; their justification by faith only (Rom 3:28) is the Reformation’s, not Trent’s.

The principle to recover is the genuinely Reformed substance of the Articles, held alongside the honest reservations of the nonconformists. The Articles confess the sufficiency of Scripture, able to make wise unto salvation (2 Tim 3:15); justification by faith alone; the sovereign election of God before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4); and the rejection of Roman corruption—real Reformation doctrine, kin to the continental confessions. Yet the English settlement retained an episcopal government and prescribed ceremonies that the Puritans, searching the Scriptures (Acts 17:11), judged to fall short of a thorough reformation by the regulative principle. The dictionary receives the Articles’ clear confession of grace and refuses both the Romeward distortion and the dead formality into which a state-church confession may decline.

etymology: Patriarch of Constantinople (fifth century), whose name is attached to the Nestorian christological error.
biblical_def: Nestorius was patriarch of Constantinople in the fifth century, whose teaching gave its name to the christological error condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431. The Nestorian error, as the church judged it, so divided the two natures of Christ—the divine and the human—as to make Him, in effect, two persons loosely joined rather than one Person in two natures. Nestorius famously objected to calling Mary Theotokos, the God-bearer or Mother of God, preferring Christotokos, mother of Christ only, on the ground that she bore the human nature, not the divine; but the church discerned that to deny that the one born of Mary was truly God in the flesh was to divide the Person of Christ. The orthodox confession, set forth at Ephesus and perfected at Chalcedon in 451, is that Christ is one Person in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion and without division—the natures distinct, yet the Person one, so that the same Christ is both the eternal Son of God and the Son of Mary, and what is true of either nature may be ascribed to the one Person. The dictionary names the Nestorian error as a corruption of the doctrine of Christ’s Person—dividing the one Christ into two—and honors the orthodox Chalcedonian confession against it: that the Word was made flesh, one Person, truly God and truly man, that He might be a fit Mediator and Saviour; for only one who is both could reconcile God and men.

corruption_summary: The Nestorian error divides Christ into two persons; Scripture and Chalcedon confess one Person, truly God and truly man, the only fit Mediator.
corruption_paragraphs: The Nestorian error is the corruption this entry names: a christology that so divides the two natures of Christ as to make Him, in effect, two persons loosely conjoined rather than one Person subsisting in two natures. Springing from the teaching of Nestorius, it recoiled from calling Mary the God-bearer, fearing to ascribe the divine to her; but in dividing the Person to guard the natures, it imperilled the truth that the one born of Mary was truly God in the flesh. The church at Ephesus discerned the danger: to divide the Person is to lose the one Christ who is both God and man.

Scripture holds the unity of Christ’s Person. The Word was made flesh (John 1:14)—not that the Word joined Himself to a separate man, but that the one eternal Son became man; in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2:9); God sent forth His Son, made of a woman (Gal 4:4). The orthodox confession, perfected at Chalcedon, is that Christ is one Person in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion and without division. This is no mere abstraction: only one who is both truly God and truly man can be the one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). To divide Christ, as the Nestorian error does, is to lose the Mediator who alone can reconcile God and sinners.

etymology: Theodoric the Great, king of the Ostrogoths (c. 454–526), an Arian ruler of Italy after the fall of Rome.
biblical_def: Theodoric the Great was king of the Ostrogoths and ruler of Italy from 493 to 526, in the generations after the fall of the western Roman Empire. A capable and, for much of his reign, tolerant ruler, he kept order, patronized learning, and let the Roman administration continue; but he was an Arian in religion, holding the heresy that denied the full and eternal deity of the Son, confessing Him a creature rather than very God of very God. Under Arian Gothic rule the orthodox Catholic population of Italy lived as subjects of a heretical king. Theodoric’s reign darkened toward its end with suspicion and persecution: he imprisoned and put to death the philosopher Boethius, who wrote his great Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, and the senator Symmachus, and he troubled the orthodox church. Theodoric stands in history as an example of the Germanic Arian kingdoms that ruled the ruins of the Roman West, holding a sub-Christian christology until they were brought, over generations, to the orthodox confession of the Son’s full deity. The dictionary names Theodoric’s Arianism as the same corruption the church condemned at Nicaea—the denial of the Son’s true and eternal Godhead—and honors the orthodox confession that prevailed against it: that the Son is of one substance with the Father, very God of very God, begotten not made, by whom all things were made.

corruption_summary: Theodoric’s Arianism is sometimes softened as mere political religion; it was the Nicene-condemned heresy that denied the Son’s true and eternal Godhead.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the tendency to soften Theodoric’s Arianism into a matter of mere political or ethnic religion—the Goths’ tribal creed, of no great doctrinal weight—or to praise his tolerance so warmly that the gravity of the heresy he held is lost. But Arianism was no trifle; it was the very error the church condemned at Nicaea in 325, the denial that the Son is true and eternal God, confessing Him instead a creature, however exalted.

The principle to recover is the full deity of the Son against the Arian denial. Scripture is plain: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God (John 1:1); by Him were all things created (Col 1:16)—and the Creator is no creature; before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58), the Son taking to Himself the divine name; we look for the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (Tit 2:13). Arianism, whether in Theodoric’s Gothic kingdom or in its modern revivals, strikes at the heart of the gospel, for a Christ who is not truly God cannot truly save. The dictionary honors the Nicene confession that prevailed: the Son is of one substance with the Father, very God of very God, begotten not made—the faith against which Theodoric’s Arianism, for all his earthly ability, stood condemned.

etymology: From local + church; the particular congregation of believers in a place, the New Testament’s ordinary sense of the church.
biblical_def: The local church is the particular congregation of professing believers gathered in a place, covenanted together under the Word, the ordinances, and the oversight of elders—the ordinary New Testament sense of the word church. The Scripture speaks of the church which was at Jerusalem, the church of God which is at Corinth, the churches of Galatia, the seven churches of Asia; these are visible, local bodies, each a true church of Christ. Distinct from the church universal—the whole company of the elect of all ages—the local church is its visible expression in a place, where the saints assemble for worship, hear the Word preached, receive baptism and the Lord’s Supper, exercise discipline, and watch over one another in love. Christ has given to the local church His officers (elders and deacons), His ordinances, and the keys of the kingdom for the receiving and excluding of members. Membership in such a church is not optional for the believer but the appointed sphere of his obedience, accountability, and growth; the New Testament knows nothing of a churchless Christian, but everywhere assumes that believers belong to and submit within a particular congregation. The dictionary honors the local church as the divinely-appointed home of the believer—the visible body where Christ is worshipped, the Word preached, the ordinances kept, and the saints watched over—against the individualism that imagines a Christianity without the church, and presses every believer to the duty and blessing of committed membership in a true congregation.

corruption_summary: The local church is treated as optional to a private Christianity; Scripture makes it the believer’s appointed home of worship, accountability, and growth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the individualist drift. The corruption is the modern individualism that imagines a Christianity without the church—a private, churchless faith of the lone believer and his God, treating membership in a congregation as optional, a matter of preference or convenience. But the New Testament knows nothing of such a Christian. It everywhere assumes that believers belong to and submit within particular, visible congregations, and it rebukes the forsaking of the assembling of ourselves together (Heb 10:25).

The principle to recover is that the local church is the divinely-appointed home and sphere of the believer’s life. The apostles ordained elders in every church (Acts 14:23); the saints at Corinth were addressed as the church of God which is at Corinth (1 Cor 1:2); to the church Christ gave the authority to receive and to exclude, so that the unrepentant is told to the church (Matt 18:17). In the local church the believer hears the Word preached, receives the ordinances, submits to the oversight of elders, is held accountable in discipline, and watches over and is watched over by the saints in love. To belong to such a church is not a Christian’s option but his calling—the appointed means of his obedience, growth, and perseverance.

etymology: From pastoral (of a shepherd) + theology; the discipline of the care and oversight of souls by the minister of Christ.
biblical_def: Pastoral theology is the discipline that treats the care and oversight of souls by the minister of Christ—the application of the whole counsel of God to the feeding, leading, guarding, and healing of the flock. Its model is the Good Shepherd, who gives His life for the sheep, knows them by name, seeks the lost, binds up the broken, and feeds them in green pastures; and its undershepherds, the elders, are charged to feed the flock of God which is among them, taking the oversight thereof not by constraint but willingly, not for filthy lucre but of a ready mind, neither as lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. The pastor’s chief work is the ministry of the Word—preaching, teaching, warning, comforting—joined to prayer, the administration of the ordinances, the visiting of the sick and the sorrowful, the admonition of the wayward, the comforting of the afflicted, and the watching for souls as one that must give account. The Reformed and Puritan tradition produced a rich literature of pastoral theology, of which Baxter’s Reformed Pastor is the great monument, pressing the minister to know and watch over every soul in his charge. The dictionary honors pastoral theology as the shepherd-care of souls after the pattern of the Chief Shepherd—the feeding, leading, guarding, and healing of the flock by the faithful minister of the Word—and presses both the high calling and the solemn account of those who watch for souls.

corruption_summary: Ministry is recast as professional management or therapeutic counsel; Scripture makes it the shepherd-care of souls by the Word, after the Chief Shepherd’s pattern.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond two drifts. The first recasts the ministry as professional management—the pastor as executive, the church as enterprise, success measured by numbers and programs. The second reduces pastoral care to therapeutic counsel, the minister a religious therapist tending felt needs with the wisdom of the age rather than the Word of God. Both displace the shepherd-care of souls by the truth, which is the heart of the office.

The principle to recover is the shepherd-care of souls after the pattern of the Chief Shepherd. The elders are charged to feed the flock of God, taking the oversight, not as lords but as ensamples (1 Pet 5:2-3), and to take heed to all the flock over which the Holy Ghost has made them overseers, to feed the church of God which He purchased with His own blood (Acts 20:28). The risen Lord’s thrice-repeated charge to Peter was, Feed my sheep (John 21:16). The pastor’s chief work is the ministry of the Word—preaching, warning, comforting—joined to prayer, the ordinances, and the watching over each soul. And the office carries a solemn account, for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account (Heb 13:17). Pastoral theology calls the minister back from the manager’s desk and the therapist’s couch to the shepherd’s staff and the Word of God.

etymology: From ministerial (of a minister) + labour; the diligent toil of the minister in the Word and in the care of the church.
biblical_def: Ministerial labour is the diligent, often costly toil of the minister of Christ in the Word and in the care of the church—the work, not the mere title or office, of those who serve as elders and preachers. Paul presses the labour of the ministry: the elders that rule well are worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine; he charges Timothy, Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth; and he describes his own ministry as labour, striving according to His working, which worketh in me mightily. The work is no light thing: the diligent study and preparation of the Word, the toil of preaching and teaching, the watching over souls, the wrestling in prayer, the bearing of the care of all the churches, the enduring of hardship and reproach. It is called a good work—if a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work—but a laborious one, demanding the whole man. The labourer is worthy of his hire, and the church is to esteem and support those who spend themselves in this toil. The dictionary honors ministerial labour as the diligent, sacrificial work of the faithful minister—in study, preaching, prayer, and the care of souls—against the notion of the ministry as ease or mere position, and presses both the minister to labour and the church to honour and uphold those who labour in the word and doctrine.

corruption_summary: The ministry is treated as ease, title, or status; Scripture makes it diligent labour in the Word and the care of souls, demanding the whole man.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the notion of the ministry as ease, title, or status—a position of honour without the toil, a platform without the study, a name without the work. But Scripture everywhere speaks of the ministry as labour. Paul does not commend the elders who merely hold office but they who labour in the word and doctrine (1 Tim 5:17), and he describes his own ministry as striving and toiling: I laboured more abundantly than they all (1 Cor 15:10).

The principle to recover is the diligent, sacrificial character of true ministerial work. The minister is a workman, charged to study to shew himself approved unto God, rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Tim 2:15)—and study, here, is no idle word but earnest toil. The work demands the whole man: the labour of preparing and preaching the Word, the wrestling in prayer, the watching over souls, the bearing of the care of the churches, the enduring of hardship. Paul labours, striving according to God’s working in him (Col 1:29). It is a good work, but a costly one. Therefore the church is to esteem and uphold those who spend themselves in it, counting them worthy of double honour, and the minister is to give himself wholly to the labour—not to the ease of office but to the toil of the Word.

word: Obey Them That Have the Rule
pronunciation: oh-BAY them that hav thuh rool
etymology: From Hebrews 13:17; the charge to submit to the elders who oversee and watch for souls in the church.
biblical_def: Obey them that have the rule over you is the charge of Hebrews concerning the believer’s duty to the elders who oversee the church: Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you. The rule spoken of is not the lordship of a tyrant but the spiritual oversight of shepherds appointed by Christ to lead, feed, and guard the flock. The believer is to obey and submit—to receive their teaching of the Word, follow their godly leading, and yield to their oversight—not blindly, for their rule is under Christ and bounded by His Word, but readily and gladly, as to those who watch for his soul and must give account for it. The same chapter bids, Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow. This submission is the appointed order of Christ’s church, by which the flock is kept and fed; and it is for the believer’s own good, for elders who must labour in grief rather than joy is unprofitable for the very souls they serve. The dictionary honors this charge as the Scripture’s call to honour and submit to the godly oversight of elders—a submission under Christ and His Word, ready and joyful, for the good of the soul—against both the lawless individualism that submits to no one and the tyranny that lords it over God’s heritage.
webster_summary: Hebrews’ charge to obey and submit to the elders who oversee the church and watch for souls; a glad submission under Christ and His Word, for the good of the soul.

corruption_summary: The charge is twisted into authoritarian control, or rejected by lawless individualism; Scripture calls for glad submission to godly oversight under Christ and His Word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond two opposite errors. The first twists the charge into authoritarian control, where elders lord it over God’s heritage, demanding unquestioning obedience and binding the conscience where Scripture has left it free—the very abuse Peter forbids when he charges elders not to be lords over God’s heritage but ensamples to the flock. The second error is the lawless individualism that rejects all oversight, submitting to no one, treating the charge to obey them that have the rule as an intrusion on personal autonomy.

The principle to recover is glad submission to godly oversight, under Christ and His Word. The rule of elders is real but bounded: it is spiritual oversight, the leading of shepherds who have spoken unto you the word of God, whose faith you are to follow (Heb 13:7), not a tyranny that binds the conscience apart from Scripture. To such oversight the believer is to obey and submit (Heb 13:17), to know and esteem those who are over him in the Lord (1 Thess 5:12), clothed with the humility that submits (1 Pet 5:5). This submission is for his own good, for elders who must watch over souls in grief rather than joy is unprofitable for those souls. The order of Christ’s church is neither tyranny nor anarchy, but the glad, humble submission of the flock to the godly oversight of shepherds who watch for souls and must give account.
roots_summary: From Hebrews 13:17; the charge to obey and submit to the elders who oversee the church and watch for souls, a glad submission under Christ and His Word.

etymology: From Ephesians 2:12; the covenant community of Israel, from which the Gentiles were once alienated and into which they are now brought in Christ.
biblical_def: The commonwealth of Israel is the covenant community of God’s people—the nation, polity, and household of faith with which God dealt under the old covenant—from which the Gentiles were once alienated, and into which they are now brought near in Christ. Paul reminds the Gentile believers what they once were: at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. To be outside the commonwealth of Israel was to be without the covenants, the promises, the law, the worship, the Messiah—strangers to all the privileges of the people of God. But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ: the middle wall of partition is broken down, and of the two, Jew and Gentile, He has made one new man, reconciling both unto God in one body by the cross. So the Gentiles are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God. The commonwealth of Israel is thus fulfilled and enlarged in the church, the Israel of God, where in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. The dictionary honors this phrase as a measure of the Gentile believer’s former misery and present mercy—once aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, now made nigh by the blood of Christ and fellow-citizens with the saints—and exalts the cross that broke the wall and made the two one.
webster_summary: The covenant community of Israel (Eph 2:12), from which the Gentiles were once aliens; now in Christ they are made nigh by His blood, fellowcitizens with the saints.
webster_full: COMMONWEALTH OF ISRAEL, the covenant community of God’s people (Eph 2:12).
The Gentiles were once aliens from it, strangers from the covenants.

Now made nigh by the blood of Christ; the middle wall broken down.
Fellowcitizens with the saints, of the household of God (Eph 2:19).

Eph 2:13

corruption_summary: The relation of Israel and the church is misread by severing them or flatly identifying them; Scripture shows the Gentiles brought into the commonwealth, the two made one in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the commonwealth of Israel and its relation to the church. The first, the dispensational severing, keeps Israel and the church as two permanently distinct peoples with separate destinies, missing Paul’s teaching that the Gentiles are brought into the commonwealth and the two made one. The second error flatly erases Israel, as though the church simply replaced a cast-off people, missing the rootedness of the church in the covenants and promises given to Israel.

The principle to recover is that in Christ the Gentiles are brought near into the covenant community, and Jew and Gentile are made one new man. Once the Gentiles were aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers from the covenants of promise, without hope and without God (Eph 2:12); but now in Christ Jesus they who were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:13). He is our peace, who hath made both one, and broken down the middle wall of partition (Eph 2:14), reconciling both unto God in one body by the cross. So the believing Gentiles are no more strangers but fellowcitizens with the saints; and the church, Jew and Gentile in one, is the Israel of God (Gal 6:16). The commonwealth of Israel is not abolished but fulfilled and enlarged in Christ, who made the two one.

etymology: From Exodus 31:18 and 34; the two tables of stone on which the LORD wrote the Ten Commandments.
biblical_def: The two tables of the law are the two tablets of stone on which the LORD wrote the Ten Commandments with His own finger and gave to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gave unto Moses two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God; and the tables were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables. When Moses, descending and seeing the golden calf, broke the first tables, the LORD commanded two new tables to be hewn, on which He wrote again the words that were in the first. The church has long understood the Ten Commandments as falling into two parts, fitly answering the two tables: the first table (the first four commandments) sets forth our duty toward God—to have no other gods, to make no graven image, not to take His name in vain, to keep the sabbath; the second table (the last six) sets forth our duty toward our neighbour—to honour father and mother, and not to kill, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet. This division is the very one the Lord gave when He summed the whole law in two commandments: to love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and thy neighbour as thyself; on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. The dictionary honors the two tables of the law as the abiding summary of human duty—love to God and love to neighbour—written by the finger of God, summed by Christ, and the rule of life for the people of God in every age.
webster_summary: The two stone tablets on which God wrote the Ten Commandments; the first table our duty to God, the second our duty to neighbour, summed by Christ in love to both.
webster_full: TWO TABLES OF THE LAW, the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments.
Written with the finger of God, given to Moses at Sinai (Exo 31:18).
The first table: our duty toward God (the first four commandments).
The second table: our duty toward neighbour (the last six).
Summed by Christ: love God, and love thy neighbour (Mat 22:40).
scriptures: And he gave unto Moses, when he had made an end of communing with him upon mount Sinai, two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God.
Exo 34:1
And the LORD said unto Moses, Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first: and I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest.
Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
corruption_summary: The law’s two tables are sundered—piety without love of neighbour, or social ethics without God; Scripture binds both, summed in love to God and neighbour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the sundering of the tables. The corruption is the sundering of the two tables—keeping the one while neglecting the other. Some embrace the first table, a piety toward God, while despising the second, the love of neighbour; James and John warn that he who loves not his brother whom he hath seen cannot love God whom he hath not seen. Others seize the second table, a social ethic of duty to man, while casting off the first, the worship and fear of God—a benevolence without the God who commands it. Both tear apart what God joined.

The principle to recover is the unity and order of the two tables, summed by Christ. The LORD wrote both with His own finger (Exo 31:18; Exo 34:1): the first table our duty toward God, the second our duty toward neighbour. And the Lord Jesus bound them together when He summed the whole law: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart (Matt 22:37), the first and great commandment, and the second like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself; on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets (Matt 22:40). The order matters: love to neighbour flows from love to God and is not its substitute. The two tables together are the abiding rule of human duty—not piety without mercy, nor mercy without piety, but love to God expressing itself in love to neighbour.

etymology: From Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8; the believer weak in faith or conscience, whom the stronger must not wound but bear.
biblical_def: The weaker brother is the believer who, weak in faith or tender in conscience, scruples over matters that Scripture has left indifferent—meats, days, and the like—and whom the stronger brother is charged to receive, bear with, and not to wound. Paul treats him in Romans and First Corinthians: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations; for one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs. The matters in view are things truly indifferent—not sins, not the plain commands of God, but disputable practices on which a tender conscience may err in scruple. The stronger brother, who rightly understands his liberty, is not to despise the weak, nor the weak to judge the strong; rather the strong is to forbear the use of his liberty where it would wound the weak brother’s conscience or embolden him to sin against it: it is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth. Love limits liberty: when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ. Yet this forbearance concerns indifferent things only; it is no license to surrender the truth of the gospel or the commands of God to another’s scruple. The dictionary honors the doctrine of the weaker brother as a charge of love—that the strong bear the infirmities of the weak, and limit their liberty for the brother’s good—against both the selfish use of liberty that wounds, and the legalism that would bind all consciences to one man’s scruple.
webster_summary: The believer weak in faith or conscience over indifferent things, whom the stronger must receive and not wound; love limits liberty for the brother’s good.
webster_full: WEAKER BROTHER, the believer weak in faith over indifferent things.

scriptures: Rom 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.
But when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ.
But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.
corruption_summary: The weaker-brother principle is stretched to bind all consciences to one scruple, or ignored by a selfish use of liberty; Scripture charges love that limits liberty in things indifferent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond two opposite abuses. The first stretches the weaker-brother principle into a tyranny of the scrupulous, by which the most easily offended conscience binds the whole church, forbidding every liberty lest someone stumble—turning Paul’s charge of love into a new legalism. But Paul’s concern is for the genuine weak brother in danger of being wounded or emboldened to sin against conscience, not for the perpetually offended who would rule others by their scruples. The second abuse is the selfish use of liberty that despises the weak and wounds them without care.

The principle to recover is love that limits liberty in things indifferent, for the brother’s good. The matters in view are truly indifferent—meats, days, disputable practices—not sins, nor the plain commands of God, nor the truths of the gospel. In these, the strong is to receive the weak, not to doubtful disputations (Rom 14:1), and to forbear his liberty where it would cause a brother to stumble: it is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth (Rom 14:21). To wound a weak brother’s conscience is to sin against Christ (1 Cor 8:12); liberty must not become a stumblingblock (1 Cor 8:9). Yet this forbearance is bounded: it concerns indifferent things, and is no license to surrender the truth of the gospel or the commands of God. Love limits liberty for the weak, but love also holds the truth fast.
